content: In two studies, students were asked to collaborate remotely using Skype-enabled devices. Junior and more experienced students worked together on real-time case studies and peer evaluations of clinical skills. These activities were generally well-received, with junior students expressing more favorable opinions in one study. Students reported that learning with smartphones in remote settings helped them form cohesive social groups and a sense of belonging. Some students noted that mobile phones allowed them to stay connected during clinical assignments. Students valued the ability to contact their supervisors remotely for discussions on patient symptoms or workplace schedules via text and chat. Emotional support was also provided through these means. However, some clinicians preferred alternative tools, such as PCs or paper, for teaching and assessments. Mobile devices were used by students and staff to organize learning activities, such as accessing clinical information or tracking academic and clinical tasks. The portability of these devices allowed students to better manage their time, especially during breaks between patient encounters or while waiting for senior staff. Mobile devices were often compared favorably to traditional textbooks, which were described as cumbersome. Students used mobile devices for reflective learning in clinical practice, repeatedly reviewing medical texts to consolidate knowledge or prepare for patient encounters. Both students and educators noted that these activities facilitated immediate or long-term insights into clinical issues. Some students reported being too busy to integrate mobile devices into their learning activities during practice. For example, they lacked time to input clinical activities for reflection or to watch online lecture videos. The use of mobile learning led to changes in pedagogy and tutor-student relationships. Students felt more confident engaging in discussions with senior colleagues due to easier access to information. Tutors described learning alongside their students. However, enthusiasm for mobile learning was not universal, with some students preferring traditional methods like paper-based learning and face-to-face communication. Students and lecturers expressed frustration with learning how to use mobile devices. Even technologically capable students were familiar with only a limited number of apps. Many relied on peers, friends, or clinical tutors for guidance. Over time, students became more comfortable with mobile devices, often through trial and error. Concerns were raised about the reliability of information distributed through mobile learning apps or websites. Students sought recommendations for apps from peers or instructors. Network connectivity was emphasized as critical, but inconsistent or poor Wi-Fi access in educational institutions and hospitals was a common issue. Mobile data plans were seen as problematic due to associated costs. When students were loaned mobile devices, these were often outdated or malfunctioning. Institutions sometimes lacked resources to provide adequate devices, leading to complaints about shared devices. Training in mobile learning was appreciated when provided, but many students reported insufficient time to familiarize themselves with devices. Technical support was described as fragmented or uncoordinated, with prolonged turnaround times for resolving issues. The implementation of mobile learning strategies was not always well-planned, with some students reporting poor timing of modules or content that did not align with their curriculum. Supervisors’ lack of device knowledge and disapproval of device use in clinical settings discouraged students from openly using mobile devices. Proposals for clear policies and behavioral etiquette for digital communication were suggested to address these challenges.
